blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Church, Elijah's work on earth was almost done, and everybody seemed to know it. Elisha had followed him for years, pouring water on his hands, learning from him. Now the old prophet kept telling him to stay behind.

verses.text: And Elijah said unto Elisha, Tarry here, I pray thee; for the LORD hath sent me to Beth-el. And Elisha said unto him, As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee. So they went down to Beth-el.

blocks.text: At Bethel, the young prophets came out and asked Elisha, do you know the LORD is taking your master today? Elisha said yes, I know. Hush. He did not want to talk about it. He wanted to stay close.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: A double portion. That was what the oldest son got from his father. Elisha was asking to carry on Elijah's work like a son carries on his father's name.

blocks.text: He called him father. Elisha watched the old man go up, and he tore his own clothes in grief.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: The old saints sang about that chariot. Swing low, sweet chariot, coming for to carry me home. Enslaved people who had nothing in this world sang about a chariot coming to carry them home. Elijah's chariot became their song of hope.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Where is the LORD God of Elijah? Elisha did not stand there wondering if God had gone up with the old prophet. He picked up the mantle, struck the water, and the water parted for him too.

blocks.speaker: narrator
blocks.text: Church, the old saints go home, and it breaks our hearts. But the God of Elijah did not leave with Elijah. The mantle falls to the next one. Pick it up, and strike the water. The same God is still here.

first_reader.note: Written by Claude in the landing session, then Claude's pastor and cultural read.

pastor.note: Faithful to 2 Kings 2:1-14 (the sons of the prophets of vv3, 5 told in words); double portion explained from Deut 21:17's sense; no promise about any listener's loved ones.

cultural.note: 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' (traditional) named as the old saints' song; grief for the elders honoured; 'I will not leave thee' at the turn.
